reference_title: Soil Stabilization and Modification for Pavements

sections.title: B-1 Acronyms
sections.summary: Defines the acronyms and abbreviations used throughout this UFC, spanning units (degC, degF, ft, g, gal, in., kg, L, lb, m, ml, mm, MPa, N, psi), chemistry (AgNO3, BaCl2, BaSO4, CaO, H2O, HCl, MgCl2), and program terms (AASHTO, ABC, ACI, DWG, FAA, LCF, LF, LIS, LL, PI, USCS).
sections.body: Acronyms used in this UFC: degC (degree Celsius), degF (degree Fahrenheit), AASHTO (American Association of State Highway and Transportation Officials), ABC (all-bituminous pavement), ACI (American Concrete Institute), AgNO3 (silver nitrate), BaCl2 (barium chloride), BaSO4 (barium sulfate), CaO (calcium oxide), DWG (Discipline Working Group), FAA (Federal Aviation Administration), ft (foot), g (gram), gal (gallon), gal/sq yd (gallon per square yard), H2O (water), HCl (hydrochloric acid), in. (inch), kg (kilogram), L (liter), lb (pound), lb/in2 (pound per square inch), LCF (lime-cement fly ash), LF (lime-fly ash), LIS (liquid injection system), LL (liquid limit), m (meter), MgCl2 (magnesium chloride), ml (milliliter), mm (millimeter), MPa (megapascal), N (Normal), pH (scale of acidity), PI (plasticity index), psi (pound per square inch), USCS (Unified Soil Classification System).
key_points: Program/organization acronyms: AASHTO, ACI, DWG (Pavements Discipline Working Group), FAA
Stabilizer-combination acronyms: LF (lime-fly ash), LCF (lime-cement-fly ash), ABC (all-bituminous pavement)
Soil property acronyms: LL (liquid limit), PI (plasticity index), USCS (Unified Soil Classification System)
Chemistry acronyms: AgNO3, BaCl2, BaSO4, CaO, H2O, HCl, MgCl2 (used in Appendix A sulfate/pH testing)

sections.title: B-2 Terms
sections.summary: Defines 8 key terms: Additive Stabilization, Additives, Durability, Mechanical Stabilization, Modification, Optimum Moisture Content, Soils, Stabilization, and Strength, distinguishing e.g. 'modification' (PI improvement, no major strength gain) from 'stabilization' (significant strength/durability increase).
sections.body: ADDITIVE STABILIZATION: stabilization achieved by adding proper percentages of additives to the soil; the type and percentage depend on soil classification, conservation of deleterious materials (sulfates, organics), and desired degree of improvement. ADDITIVES: manufactured commercial products that improve engineering characteristics when added in proper quantities; 'traditional' additives include lime, cement, fly ash, asphalt emulsions; 'non-traditional' additives include polymer emulsions, fiber, lignin derivatives, enzymes, acids, and other materials. Additives addressed in this UFC: portland cement, lime, fly ash, bitumen, polymer emulsion, fiber, and select combinations. DURABILITY: resistance of the soil to weathering, primarily by water action and abrasion after wet-dry and freezing-thawing cycles (ASTM D559 and D560). MECHANICAL STABILIZATION: accomplished by mixing/blending soils of two or more gradations to meet a required specification, then spreading and compacting; compaction (mechanical rearrangement of soil particles into a denser configuration) and fiber addition are also forms of mechanical stabilization. MODIFICATION: a stabilization process improving a material property (e.g. PI) but NOT, by design, resulting in a significant increase in soil strength and durability. OPTIMUM MOISTURE CONTENT: the water content (percentage by unit weight) at which a maximum dry unit weight can be achieved for a given compactive effort (ASTM D1557); a higher or lower moisture content yields a lower maximum dry unit weight. SOILS: naturally occurring materials used for construction of all pavement layers except surface layers (concrete/asphalt), subject to classification testing (ASTM D2487). STABILIZATION: the process of blending/mixing materials with soil to improve engineering properties -- may blend soils for gradation or mix additives to alter chemistry, gradation, texture, plasticity, water absorption, or provide cementation; RESULTS IN A SIGNIFICANT INCREASE in strength and/or durability of the material (this is the key distinction from 'modification'). STRENGTH: in this UFC, refers to unconfined compressive strength measured per ASTM D1633.
key_points: Stabilization vs. Modification: stabilization causes a SIGNIFICANT strength/durability increase; modification improves a property (e.g. PI) without that significant increase
Mechanical stabilization: blending soils of different gradations, OR compaction, OR fiber addition (not a chemical additive process)
Durability: resistance to weathering per wet-dry (ASTM D559) and freeze-thaw (ASTM D560) cycling
Optimum Moisture Content: the moisture giving maximum dry unit weight for a given compactive effort (ASTM D1557)
Strength (as used in this UFC) specifically means unconfined compressive strength (ASTM D1633)
sections.applicability: Reference lookup for the precise engineering meaning of key terms (especially the stabilization/modification distinction) used throughout this UFC.
